tldr: This paper presents a robot policy that is robust to delays and sampling frequency jitter by explicitly feeding sensor capture times and action execution times into the model as physical timestamps and directly coupling attention to elapsed physical time using Time-aware RoPE.
hero_caption: An overview of temporal jitter in robot systems. It shows the impact of various timing offsets—such as sensor sampling rates, communication delays, inference latency, and control periods—on dynamic tasks (observation-to-action timing), multisensory tasks (relative timing between observations), and quasi-static tasks (train-test mismatch).
overview:
In conventional imitation learning, sensor observations and robot commands are treated as fixed-rate sequences, implicitly using sequence position (index) as a proxy for the passage of time. In the real world, however, physical time is always fluctuating due to camera frame drops, communication delays, and inference latency jitter. Even with the same two-frame difference, object velocity differs tenfold depending on whether the interval is 20ms or 200ms. Furthermore, if the policy does not know how many milliseconds later the motor will actually execute a predicted command, it cannot accurately grasp a moving object.

To address this, the authors propose Chronos Policy, which explicitly provides the policy with the physical time when observations were captured and the future physical time when actions should be executed. The key idea is using Time-aware RoPE—an extension of rotary position embeddings grounded in physical time—rather than simply adding timestamp embeddings to token features. This allows attention weights to depend directly on the physical time differences between observations and actions without corrupting token content. Furthermore, during training, the sampling intervals and the start delay of action chunks are temporally randomized, allowing the policy to learn directly from unaligned multisensory data and adapt to real-world timing variations.

Evaluation was conducted across dynamic object tracking, multi-sensor pivoting, standard manipulation benchmarks, and real robot experiments. While conventional Diffusion Policy suffers severe performance drops under inference delays and sampling variations, Chronos Policy maintains very high success rates, demonstrating overwhelming robustness against temporal variations.
contributions: Formulated a robot policy learning framework operating on physical time by conditioning on observation capture times and desired action execution times.

Developed a diffusion transformer incorporating Time-aware RoPE into rotary position embeddings, enabling direct learning from asynchronous, multi-rate sensors without resampling onto a fixed temporal grid.
Constructed benchmarks mimicking realistic temporal variations and demonstrated improved robustness in dynamic and multisensory control across simulation and real robot experiments.

sections.heading: Robot Clocks Are Not Constant: From Sequence Order to Physical Time
sections.summary: In real robot environments, sensor capture intervals and inference latency constantly fluctuate, causing conventional methods that substitute sequence index for time to break down. This work proposes Chronos Policy, which explicitly feeds exact physical timestamps of observations and actions and captures time differences directly via Time-aware RoPE.
sections.details:
Real-world robot systems never operate on a constant clock. Consider a robot grasping an object moving along a conveyor belt. Even if the object travels the exact same distance across two consecutive image frames, its true physical velocity differs completely depending on whether the frame interval was 20ms or 200ms. Similarly, the required target hand position changes depending on whether the predicted action will be executed right now or 100ms later.

Despite this, most conventional imitation learning approaches convert demonstrations into fixed-rate sequence data and treat the sequence index (the data position) as physical time. When sampling rates fluctuate or inference delays occur, the policy cannot determine how much time elapsed between observations or how far in the future the predicted actions will be executed.

While prior works have attempted targeted compensations for inference latency, this work takes a different approach. Rather than treating timing offsets as external errors to be patched after the fact, it explicitly formulates when observations were captured ($t_o$) and when actions are desired to execute ($t_a$) as model inputs.

A crucial design decision here is how to inject time information into the network. One could add timestamp embeddings to token features, but that entangles what was observed with when it was observed. Instead, this work preserves token content intact and adopts Time-aware RoPE (rotary position embeddings) to compute attention over physical time. This makes attention depend directly on elapsed time differences ($t_i - t_j$), enabling stable representations that do not rely on an arbitrary time reference point (clock origin).

sections.heading: Prior Work on Asynchronous Multisensory Learning and Delay Compensation
sections.summary: This section reviews related work across asynchronous learning for varying sensor rates, action chunking methods to bridge inference latency, and continuous-time attention mechanisms. Chronos Policy is unique in unifying observation and action sequences directly on physical time.
sections.details:
### Asynchronous Multisensory Learning
Contact-rich tasks require combining slow vision with high-frequency tactile or force-torque sensing. Prior approaches have processed them with separate modules or integrated policies operating at sensor-specific inference rates. However, these are specialized tricks to exploit high-frequency feedback rather than a unified treatment of overall time.

### Inference Latency and Action Chunk Continuity
As policies scale up, processing images and inferring actions introduces non-negligible latency. To smoothly stitch predicted action chunks on physical hardware, studies have conditioned on past scheduled actions or used inpainting. Other works focus on reducing inference steps for lower latency. Chronos Policy does not aim to speed up inference; instead, it treats the remaining latency as an explicit time parameter, making it complementary to acceleration techniques.

### Explicit Time in Robot Control and Continuous-Time Attention
Prior work has fed remaining task time into policies to modulate execution speed, while research in NLP and video generation has explored continuous-time attention and extensions of RoPE (Rotary Position Embeddings) for irregular time series. This work introduces this continuous-time perspective into robot imitation learning, unifying capture times of heterogeneous sensors and future action execution times into a single framework.

sections.heading: Learning with Time-aware RoPE and Temporal Randomization
sections.summary: Chronos Policy is based on a Diffusion Transformer and embeds observation capture times and desired action execution times using Time-aware RoPE. During training, sampling intervals and execution start delays are randomized, directly tying attention to relative elapsed time without modifying token content.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Policy Formulation on Physical Time
Let $\mathbf{O}_{\mathbf{t}_o}$ denote observations captured at times $\mathbf{t}_o$. Given a query request time $t$, an action chunk of $H$ steps is queried at the following execution times:
$$\mathbf{t}_a = \{t + d_t + j\Delta t_a\}_{j=0}^{H-1}$$
where $d_t$ is the delay before the first action executes (e.g., inference latency) and $\Delta t_a$ is the action execution interval. The policy is formulated as $\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{t}_a} \sim \pi(\cdot \mid \mathbf{O}_{\mathbf{t}_o}, \mathbf{t}_o, \mathbf{t}_a)$. In this way, observation rates, sensor delays, inference latency, and required execution frequencies are all made explicit as timing parameters.

### 3.2 Encoding Physical Time with Time-aware RoPE
To incorporate time into the model, the method does not add timestamp embeddings to token features. Instead, it uses physical time as positional encodings for attention. Each token is assigned a relative time $\tilde{t} = t' - t$ with respect to the request time $t$. For action tokens, $\tilde{t}_{a,j} = d_t + j\Delta t_a$, meaning inference delay is naturally expressed as a forward time shift.
By using these relative times as rotation coordinates for actions and observations, the inner product between query $q_i$ and key $k_j$ depends solely on elapsed time $t_j - t_i$:
$$(R(\tilde{t}_i) q_i)^\top (R(\tilde{t}_j) k_j) = q_i^\top R(t_j - t_i) k_j$$
In other words, even if two observations are adjacent in sequence tokens, attention propagation naturally varies with physical time depending on whether the interval was 20ms or 200ms.

### 3.3 Training with Temporal Randomization
During training, the sampling rates, delivery delays, and action chunk start delay $d_t$ are randomly varied when drawing observations from demonstrations. Because timestamps are explicit, varying intervals does not introduce ambiguity, allowing full utilization of data that would otherwise be discarded when downsampling to a fixed rate. Training uses the standard $\ell_1$ loss of diffusion models.

### 3.4 Deployment on Real Robots
The same interface is used during deployment. Since exact inference latency is unknown beforehand on real robots, $d_t$ is estimated from the completion time of the previous request. Any predicted actions within the chunk whose execution times have already passed are discarded, and the remaining actions are executed asynchronously.

captions.F2: Overall pipeline of Chronos Policy. (a) Observations and action queries from sensors with different rates and delays are (b) encoded via Time-aware RoPE using physical-time-based rotation matrices $R(t)$, ensuring that (c) attention along a shared physical timeline depends solely on elapsed time differences.

sections.heading: The Power of Time Awareness Demonstrated in Simulation and Real Robots
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted across a dynamic conveyor task, a multisensory pivoting task, six quasi-static DexMimicGen tasks, and real robot experiments. Chronos Policy prevented performance collapse under severe inference delays and sampling variations, exhibiting high robustness.
sections.details:
The experiments address three main questions: (1) what tasks benefit from temporal information, (2) which policy components matter, and (3) whether there is any penalty on tasks where timing is less critical.

### 4.1 & 4.2 Dynamic and Multisensory Tasks
In the dynamic Conveyor task, observation-to-action timing is crucial. While standard Diffusion Policy success plummeted to just 1.8% under inference delays up to 200ms, Chronos Policy maintained 76.4%. In the Combined condition with both observation variations and delays, where the baseline dropped to 0.0%, Chronos Policy achieved 32.7%.
Similar results were observed in Pivoting, which integrates tactile, force-torque, and vision. Under 200ms delay, Chronos Policy achieved 60.2% versus 51.3% for the baseline; under Combined conditions, it achieved 38.4% versus 19.6%, demonstrating notable resilience to inter-sensor timing offsets.

### 4.3 Ablation: What Makes It Work?
The authors compared temporal randomization during training and time embedding methods (AddTime vs RoPE).
- Temporal randomization alone: Randomizing timing without timestamps acted as data augmentation on simple tasks like Conveyor, but in Pivoting it blurred physical sequence meaning, significantly degrading success from 48.4% to 21.6%. It produced consistent gains (55.3%) only when combined with timestamps.
- AddTime vs Time-aware RoPE: Compared to additive Fourier embeddings (AddTime), Time-aware RoPE performed substantially better under harsh variations: 32.7% vs 7.8% on Conveyor, and 38.4% vs 16.7% on Pivoting. This validates separating token content from time and measuring elapsed time directly through attention.

### 4.4 Impact on Quasi-Static Tasks
Across six standard DexMimicGen manipulation tasks, Chronos Policy matched baseline performance under nominal conditions and improved average success from 59.7% to 73.4% under timing variations. Thus, there is no downside to explicit time conditioning even when timing is not critical.

### 4.5 Real-World Robot Experiments
Evaluations covered three tasks: Dynamic Cup, Peg Insertion, and Pivoting. Compared against Real-Time Chunking (RTC), a prior delay mitigation technique, Chronos Policy achieved the highest score across all tasks and conditions. While RTC handles inference delay, it cannot address observation-side timing variations; Chronos Policy unifies both observation and action timing, overcoming compound timing jitter in real-world environments.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Future Directions: Towards Adjustable Robot Speed
sections.summary: This work demonstrated that making observation and action timing explicit enables learning policies that are exceptionally robust to temporal jitter. Future directions include moving beyond fixed-rate action chunks to dynamically scaling robot execution speed faster or slower than demonstrations.
sections.details:
This paper proposed Chronos Policy, anchoring robot imitation learning to physical time by conditioning on observation capture times and action execution times. This framework unifies sensor sampling frequency differences, delivery delays, and inference latency within a single policy.

Across dynamic, multisensory, and quasi-static tasks in simulation and real robots, the approach confirmed dramatic resilience to temporal mismatch without sacrificing nominal performance.

Future work includes supporting variable action output frequencies beyond fixed rates (e.g., 20Hz), as well as scaling temporal duration to execute demonstrations faster or more cautiously and slowly on demand.

sections.heading: Appendix: Network Architecture and Experimental Details
sections.summary: The model uses SigLIP2 and a 16-layer Diffusion Transformer, combining self-attention across non-image tokens with cross-attention to image tokens. In real-robot setups, high-frequency sensors like a ~360Hz force-torque sensor are naturally handled via strided sampling.
sections.details:
### Model Architecture Details
The base model is a Diffusion Transformer with width 512, 8 heads, and 16 layers. Image features are extracted using a pretrained SigLIP2-base encoder, projecting 768-dimensional patch tokens from $256\times 256$ resolution into the transformer.
Proprioception, force-torque, and noisy action vectors are embedded as separate tokens. Non-image tokens interact via self-attention, and cross-attention is applied to image tokens. Time-aware RoPE rotates 16 pairs of query-key coordinates with frequencies logarithmically spaced between 0.1s and 2s.

### Training and Hardware Setup
The loss function is the $\ell_1$ loss on action predictions, trained with AdamW at a learning rate of $3\times 10^{-4}$ with a cosine schedule for 50 epochs.
In real-robot tasks such as Peg Insertion and Pivoting, fingertip force-torque data recorded at ~360Hz is sampled with stride 4, serving as a ~90Hz history. Unlike prior approaches that force all sensors onto a shared slow temporal grid, each modality can be learned directly with its native capture timestamps—a major practical benefit of Chronos Policy.

captions.F6: Detailed network diagram of Chronos Policy. Proprioception, force-torque, and action tokens attend to each other via self-attention and to image patches via cross-attention. Time-aware RoPE is applied to all tokens, performing iterative denoising conditioned on physical time.

takeaways: In sequence models for robot control, assuming token index substitutes for time easily breaks down under real-world delays and jitter.

When incorporating physical time, encoding it as relative attention coordinates (Time-aware RoPE) is far more robust than adding it to token features (AddTime) because it leaves token content uncorrupted.
Temporal randomization data augmentation boosts generalization without collapsing multisensory policies only when paired with explicit timestamps.
Asynchronous and multi-rate sensor streams can be learned and integrated directly with native timestamps without forcing them onto a fixed-rate grid.
limitations: The control frequency within predicted action chunks remains fixed, and actively scaling execution speed dynamically is not yet implemented.
Real-world deployment relies on estimating inference latency $d_t$ from previous completion times, limiting accuracy during sudden, sharp inference spikes.
While handling high-frequency sensor streams natively is supported, increased token counts introduce a computational cost trade-off within the Transformer.
